summary: This document defines an extension to the Netnews article format that can authenticate the withdrawal of existing articles. It updates RFC 5537. Only the original poster or authorized parties can then cancel a post.

plainLanguage.summary: Only the person with the key can delete their post, like putting a padlock on it that only the owner can open.

questions: how to authenticate netnews article cancellation
how does netnews cancel authentication work
subtitle: A hash-based padlock that lets only the original poster, or an authorized agent, cancel or replace a Netnews article.

tldr.problem: Netnews lets articles be withdrawn with a cancel control article or a Supersedes header field, but servers need a simple way to check that the withdrawal was requested by someone legitimate.
tldr.mechanism: The original article carries a Cancel-Lock header holding hashes of secret keys. The withdrawal carries a Cancel-Key header with the key itself, and servers hash it and compare.
tldr.outcome: A match shows the withdrawal was approved by a legitimate person or agent. It gives no integrity or originator guarantees, and it updates RFC 5537.

facts.label: Recommended secret length
facts.value: at least 256 bits / 32 octets for SHA256

today: RFC 8315 is a Proposed Standard (February 2018) that updates RFC 5537. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Cancel-Lock Idea
sections.content:
This is a simple method to verify that withdrawing a Netnews article is valid. The poster, posting agent, moderator or injecting agent that processed the original article must have requested the withdrawal, using a cancel control article or a Supersedes header field (RFC 5537).

It defines two header fields. Cancel-Lock holds hashes of secret data. The preimages are later given in Cancel-Key to authenticate a cancel or supersede request. One stated property is that it prevents tracking of individual users. When everybody must be able to verify the originator, an OpenPGP signature is appropriate instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock goes on your post when you send it. The key is only shown later, when you want to take the post down.

sections.title: The Two Header Fields
sections.content:
Each header field MUST NOT occur more than once in an article. Both contain lists of entries of the form scheme:string. The schemes defined are sha256 and sha512, and sha256 is mandatory to implement. Implementations SHOULD NOT generate sha224 or sha384.

A c-lock is Base64(hash(Base64(K))) for a secret key K, so K is not revealed. A c-key is Base64(K). Entries with an unsupported scheme MUST be skipped, and later entries MUST NOT be ignored. Comments SHOULD NOT be generated but MUST be accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock is a scrambled fingerprint of a secret. The key is the secret itself. Scrambling is easy, but unscrambling is not.

sections.title: Who Adds and Checks Them
sections.content:
A poster or posting agent MAY add a Cancel-Lock with one or more entries. If none was added, an injecting agent or moderator MAY add one. Later agents up to the injecting agent MAY append entries. Once injected, the field MUST NOT be altered, and relaying agents beyond the injecting agent MUST NOT alter it. Each entry added by one agent MUST use a unique key K.

A Cancel-Key MAY be added to a proto-article that has a Control or Supersedes header field. An injecting agent or moderator acting for a poster who cannot do this MUST be able to positively authenticate the poster.

To check, a server hashes each supported c-key with its own scheme and compares it to each c-lock with the same scheme in the original article. One match means authentication passes. If the new article has no Cancel-Key or the original has no Cancel-Lock, authentication is not possible. The general handling in RFC 5537 is not changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The news server takes the key you show, scrambles it the same way, and sees whether it matches the lock on the post. If it matches, you may remove the post.

sections.title: Calculating the Key
sections.content:
The RECOMMENDED way to get the key is K = HMAC(sec, uid+mid) (RFC 2104), where sec is a local secret, uid is a User-ID and mid is the article's Message-ID, including the angle brackets. This avoids a per-article database of keys. The User-ID must not contain angle brackets, and an agent with a dedicated secret per user should use an empty uid.

The secret should be at least the hash output size (256 bits, or 32 octets, for SHA256) and must be a cryptographically random value. The hash behind the HMAC need not match the scheme. If one agent adds several locks, different secrets must be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of remembering a new key for every post, you mix one master secret with the post's name. Only you can redo that mix later.

sections.title: Worked Examples and Obsolete Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC gives OpenSSL command-line examples, with and without a UID. For article <12345@mid.example> and secret ExampleSecret, the key is qv1VXHYiCGjkX/N1nhfYKcAeUn8bCVhrWhoKuBSnpMA=, and its lock is sha256:s/pmK/3grrz++29ce2/mQydzJuc7iqHn1nqcJiQTPMc=. Scheme parsing must be case insensitive.

Earlier drafts used sha1 as the scheme and a looser key syntax. sha1 is deprecated and SHOULD NOT be generated, though servers SHOULD still accept it for a transition period while the hash is not considered unsafe or marked OBSOLETE. The loose key syntax SHOULD NOT be generated but MUST be accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: The document shows step by step how to make a lock and its matching key, so you can check your own work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The system provides no integrity checking. An article can be modified in transit whether or not a Cancel-Key is present. A matching key only says the withdrawal was approved by a legitimate person or agent. A valid key lifted from a cancel article could be pasted into a forged supersede, but forged identity information is already possible without any authentication. For originator and integrity checks, a signature system such as OpenPGP is needed, and both can be combined.

Preimage resistance of the hash matters most. Collision resistance matters less. Because Cancel-Key values are published, an attacker who breaks the HMAC and recovers the secret could forge requests for every article locked with it, so changing the secret at regular intervals can limit damage. SHA2 was chosen over SHA1 because the previous specification is nearly two decades old and SHA1 collision resistance is already broken.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock proves a person is allowed to remove a post. It does not stop someone from tampering with the post on its way, and it does not prove who wrote it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the Cancel-Lock and Cancel-Key header fields for the netnews protocol. It also maintains a "Netnews Cancel-Lock Hash Algorithms" registry on a First Come First Served basis, with names made of letters, digits, hyphens and slashes.

Initial entries: sha256 and sha512 are COMMON; sha1, sha224 and sha384 are LIMITED USE; md5 is OBSOLETE. Registrations MUST NOT be deleted, but can be marked OBSOLETE.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of the scrambling methods allowed, and each one is marked as good, so-so or do-not-use.

items.label: OBSOLETE
items.desc: Do not use this algorithm anymore.
